title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI systems were used to create a fabricated interview impersonating a real finance presenter and central bank governor to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The system produced not just a deepfake of the individuals but an entire false news article presenting the interview as factual reporting, deployed directly to potential victims without any human verification that the content was authentic or that the endorsement existed.

This is impersonation at scale enabled by generative AI. The fraud worked by combining a false model output with a fabricated news article format to create an appearance of legitimacy. It would have been caught by basic verification: checking whether the interview actually aired, confirming the governor's actual position on the platform, or verifying the news outlet's records. Instead the scam relied on speed and volume, with regulatory data showing that such impersonation frauds are now common enough to constitute what Australian regulators describe as a growing systemic threat.

It is not established what specific AI tools or models were used to create the content or how they were trained.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake article recently circulated online featuring a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview, which depicted Bullock storming out over Kohler's questions, never actually occurred. This type of scam represents a growing threat, with Australia's financial regulator ASIC reporting a significant surge in AI-generated investment fraud using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive consumers.

ASIC's latest research reveals that scam takedowns increased by 182 percent last year, with fake investment platforms rising 151 percent and phishing scams jumping 279 percent. High-profile Australians commonly impersonated include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, businessman Dick Smith, and mining magnate Gina Rinehart. Scammers now create elaborate deception networks featuring fake news articles, reviews, and advertisements to build credibility. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and to be skeptical of celebrity endorsements or offers that seem too good to be true.
